title: How do I stop catastrophizing? What helps when your mind jumps to the worst case
description: Why an unanswered message becomes a film about losing everything — catastrophizing is a chain of 'what if' steps that inflates how likely and how bad an outcome feels while rating your coping at zero — and what helps in order: write the chain down, separate likelihood, badness and coping, name the unknown, postpone the spiral, and practise the most-likely version.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

It starts with something small and genuinely uncertain. A message that has not been answered. A pain that was not there yesterday. A meeting added to the calendar with no agenda. Within a minute the mind is no longer on the message, the pain or the meeting. It is three steps past them: the friendship is ending, the illness is serious, the job is gone — and then three steps past that. Each step arrives as a question — "what if…?" — and each answer becomes the starting point for a worse question. By the time the chain stops, you are not frightened of what happened. You are frightened of a film that has not happened, may never happen, and feels, in your body, as if it already has. If you have searched "how to stop catastrophizing" or "why do I always think the worst", this guide is for that moment. It sets out what the research actually shows about how the worst-case chain is built, what helps in the order most people can use it, and where an app honestly fits. We print our own numbers as they are, small as they are.

We are Anicca. We make a small affirmation app; inside it, you choose the struggles you are in — stress, overthinking, a hard day — and short cards on those topics arrive through the day. This guide is not an advertisement, and it is not treatment. Catastrophizing is not a diagnosis. It is a thinking habit — one of the most closely studied in cognitive therapy — and a habit of thought has parts, and the parts can be examined, and interrupted, separately.

## Why does your mind jump to the worst case?

Four findings from the research do most of the work here.

**First, the worst case is rarely one thought. It is a chain, and the chain has a measurable shape.** In a classic experiment, Vasey and Borkovec asked chronic worriers and nonworriers to follow one of their own worries through a sequence of "what if…?" steps — a catastrophizing assessment modelled on the cognitive-therapy technique of decatastrophising, run in reverse. The worriers generated significantly more catastrophic steps than the nonworriers. Their subjective discomfort rose significantly as the catastrophizing progressed, while the nonworriers' did not. And they rated the events in their own sequences as significantly more likely to actually occur. With few exceptions, the content of the two groups' chains did not differ. Read that carefully, because it is the most hopeful finding on this page: the worrier's imagination is not made of darker material. The difference is length and belief — more steps, each one felt as more probable. A chain is a process, not a prophecy, and a process can be interrupted at any link. Davey and Levy, studying catastrophic worrying directly, added a second feature: a perseverative, iterative style — the same questioning loop applied again and again — and a tendency to frame the steps in terms of personal inadequacy, so that the chain quietly changes subject, from "what might happen" to "what is wrong with me, that it will happen to me".

**Second, two separate judgements are inflated at once — how likely the bad outcome is, and how bad it would be.** Butler and Mathews showed early on that anxious individuals gave higher subjective probability ratings to negative, threatening events — specifically when those events were predicted for themselves rather than for some other person. The same event, on the same evidence: more likely, if it is happening to me. The cost side is inflated alongside the probability side in the judgemental-bias literature: the outcome is rated not only likelier but more awful. Catastrophizing is the two inflations multiplied — a future that is probably not coming, priced as if it were both certain and unendurable. That is why arguing with only one side ("it probably won't happen") so often fails to settle anything. The other side ("but if it did, it would be the end") is still standing, untouched.

**Third, when researchers broke catastrophizing into parts, it separated into three — and each part points at a different counter-move.** Sullivan, Bishop and Pivik built the Pain Catastrophizing Scale in the pain field, where this habit has been measured most carefully: 13 items, rated from 0 ("not at all") to 4 ("all the time"), which separated into rumination ("I can't seem to keep it out of my mind" — the thought will not leave), magnification (the threat value of the situation is exaggerated — it looms larger than its size), and helplessness ("there is nothing I can do to reduce it" — coping is rated at zero). In the original analysis, the rumination component accounted for 41% of the total variance, magnification for 10% and helplessness for 8%. The scale was built for pain, and this guide is not about pain. But the three-part shape travels, because everyday worst-case thinking shows the same joints: a loop that will not stop, a threat drawn too big, and a self drawn too small to cope. The steps below are organised against those three parts: stop the loop growing, re-measure the threat, and restore the coping side of the ledger.

**Fourth, the fuel is usually not danger. It is not knowing — and the body's alarm, misread as evidence.** In an experiment by Ladouceur, Talbot and Dugas, 49 people completed inference tasks at different levels of ambiguity. Intolerance of uncertainty — finding it unacceptable that a negative event might occur, however small its probability — was related to needing more cues before deciding, specifically in the moderately ambiguous task: the everyday kind of situation, not clear and not hopeless, just unresolved. When Buhr and Dugas experimentally increased people's fear of anxiety itself, worry rose — and increased fear of anxiety combined with intolerance of uncertainty produced the highest worry of all. The body completes the circuit. Clark's cognitive model of panic proposed that panic attacks result from the catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations — palpitations read as an impending heart attack, breathlessness as collapse — where the misreading raises anxiety, the raised anxiety produces more sensations, and the new sensations are misread in turn. You do not need panic for a smaller version of that loop to run: an uncertain situation, a body that reacts, and a mind that reads its own reaction as proof that the worst case must be near.

## What helps, in the order most people can use it

### 1. Write the chain down — the trigger, the "what if", and where it ends

Before arguing with the chain, make it visible. Take the worry that is currently running and write it the way the researchers elicited it: the trigger on the first line ("no reply to my message since Tuesday"), then each "what if…?" as its own line, in the order your mind produced them, down to the final frame the chain ends on. Two things become visible on paper that are invisible inside the spiral. The first is length: this is step seven of a chain that began with an unanswered message, and the distance between line one and line seven is the size of the leap your mind made without showing you. The second is the subject change Davey and Levy described: somewhere around the middle, most chains stop being about the event and start being about the self — "and then everyone will see I can't cope". Mark that line when you find it. It is not information about the future; it is the inadequacy frame arriving on schedule. And hold onto the Vasey and Borkovec result while you look at the page: discomfort rose with each step while the content stayed ordinary. Feeling worse at step seven is data about the chain. It is not data about what is going to happen.

### 2. Separate the three judgements — how likely, how bad, and how you would cope

The classic decatastrophising questions work because they refuse to let the three inflated judgements hide inside one feeling. Take the final frame from Step 1 and answer, in writing, one question per part. How likely is it, really? Write three outcomes side by side — the worst, the best, and the most likely — and give the most likely one a number out of 100. Butler and Mathews' finding is the reason for the number: your first estimate is a self-referential judgement, measurably inflated when the event is aimed at you, and a written number can be argued with in a way a feeling cannot. How bad would it be, and for how long? Not "unbearable" — concretely: what would the week after it look like, what would still be intact, would it still be the main fact of your life in a year? And how would you cope? Name the first thing you would do, the person you would call, and one hard thing you have already got through. In the spiral, helplessness is rated at zero by default; on paper, it almost never is zero. None of this is positive thinking. The worst case stays on the page, in full. It is simply priced accurately — likely, bad, copable — instead of infinitely: certain, total, and beyond you.

### 3. Ask what you would need to know — and notice when "not knowing" is the fuel

Next, name the unknown itself, precisely: not "the situation" but the specific fact that is missing ("whether the results are back", "whether she is angry or just busy"). Then ask the deciding question: is there information that would actually change what I do next? If there is, take the one concrete step that gets it — send the message, book the appointment, ask the question — and let the chain wait for facts. One boundary matters here, and it runs in both directions: a new, changing or persistent physical symptom is information to get checked medically, not an uncertainty to practise tolerating, and no step in this guide outranks that. But if the honest answer is that the fact cannot be known yet — it arrives Thursday, it depends on someone else, it may never be fully knowable — then say that sentence out loud: "This cannot be known before Thursday." Ladouceur and colleagues' result explains why the sentence helps: the moderately ambiguous situation is exactly the one that keeps the mind demanding more cues, and naming the ambiguity as the trigger re-attributes the alarm. The alarm is being produced by not knowing. It is not extra evidence about the outcome — and Buhr and Dugas' experiment adds the second half: fear of the anxiety itself is fuel, so a racing heart during the wait is the loop running, not the future leaking information.

### 4. Postpone the spiral — give worry one time and one place

A chain that can start anywhere will start everywhere, so shrink where it is allowed to run. This is the oldest technique on this page: the stimulus control of worry, first described by Borkovec and colleagues in 1983. Its instructions are simple. Learn to catch a worry as it starts. Postpone it — note it in a few words, and return your attention to what is in front of you. Keep one worry period, about half an hour, at the same time and in the same place each day, and during that period, worry on purpose about the noted concerns, and problem-solve the ones you can actually act on. The evidence is modest and we report it that way: in a preliminary investigation, McGowan and Behar randomly assigned 53 people with high trait worry to two weeks of this training or to a comparison condition, and the stimulus control group showed larger reductions in worry, anxiety and insomnia. Fifty-three people and two weeks is a beginning, not a proof. Postponement is also not suppression, and the difference matters: nothing here asks you to forbid the thought or win an argument with it. You are keeping an appointment with it. Many chains, when their appointment arrives, have lost their urgency or been answered by events — and the ones that have not are waiting on paper, in one place, where Step 2 can be applied to them properly.

### 5. Practise the most-likely version — small, repeated, at a believable size

Finally, give the mind a competing sentence to rehearse, built from Step 2's work: the most-likely outcome plus the coping step, in one line — "Most likely the results are routine and I hear on Thursday; if they are not, the first thing I do is call the clinic and ask what happens next." Two construction rules. Keep it at a size you can believe on a bad evening: "everything will be fine" fails the size test, because the mind cross-examines it and returns with the chain, longer. And repeat it at the moment the chain starts, not after it has run — the sentence is a replacement for step two of the chain, not a verdict delivered at step nine. Expect the practice to feel deliberate for a while. The habit research gives the realistic scale: when Lally and colleagues modelled how long new behaviours take to feel automatic, the median was 66 days, with a wide range from 18 to 254 days. Judge this across several weeks of spirals — are the chains shorter, do you catch them earlier — rather than by whether one bad night went quietly.

## Where do apps fit in this?

An affirmation app cannot change a probability, cannot know the unknown fact before Thursday, and cannot sit with you through the bad outcome if it comes. What it can do, at most, is supply words at the two moments this guide depends on words: the moment the chain starts (Step 5's sentence, which is precisely the sentence you cannot produce at step seven of a spiral) and the postponement moment (Step 4, when a noted worry needs somewhere to wait that is not your working memory). Used that way, it belongs inside the steps: one card, read slowly, built from your own most-likely version — "the results come Thursday, and I have a first step either way" — rather than a generic promise that nothing bad will happen, which your mind will correctly reject. Used as another feed to scroll at 2 a.m., it is not a competing sentence; it is more chain material.

What to check before you rely on any app for this: whether you can choose the struggle you are in (overthinking, stress, a hard day) rather than receiving the same generic lines as everyone else; whether the words are sized to be believed at your most frightened, not just pleasant at your calmest; whether it reaches you during the day, when the chains actually start, instead of only when you remember to open it; and what it costs, in full, after any trial. Anicca is built around those choices: you pick the struggles, and short cards on those topics arrive through the day. That is a design claim, not a result. The measured part is the next section.

## Our own numbers, printed as they are

Anicca is small, and we publish the smallness. When we checked in November 2026, its US App Store listing showed 5.0 stars from 1 rating, and its Japanese listing 4.5 stars from 48 ratings. App Store Connect recorded 1 first download for Anicca in the 7 days to 12 November 2026. Premium is $59.99 a year on the US listing. If social proof is what you need — and for something you would open in the middle of a worst-case spiral it is a reasonable thing to need — larger apps have it and we do not, yet. What we can claim is only the design: a short card, on the topic you chose, arriving while the day is happening. Whether that design helps anyone interrupt a catastrophizing chain is exactly what our numbers are still too small to show.

## When is catastrophizing a sign to get human help?

Catastrophizing is a style of thinking, not a diagnosis, and a person who runs worst-case chains is not thereby ill. The style becomes a reason to get human help when it stops being occasional and starts organising a life. If worry runs for most of the day, most days, over months, and you cannot postpone it even briefly; if you are avoiding places, messages, appointments or medical results because of what the chain says they might mean, and your world is getting smaller; if the bodily loop described by Clark is completing into panic attacks; if checking, searching and asking for reassurance are taking hours; or if your sleep is broken night after night by chains that will not close — treat that as a reason to talk to a clinician, not as a reason to try harder at a guide like this one. Generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder, health anxiety, OCD and depression are diagnosable, treatable conditions in which these exact processes are central, and the treatments for them work on the chain with a person, at a depth an article cannot reach. The physical boundary also bears repeating: new, changing or persistent symptoms deserve a medical check on their own merits — decatastrophising is for the interpretation of your life, never a substitute for examining your body. If you ever feel that you might act on thoughts of harming yourself, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line in your country now — in Japan, call 110 or 119 in an emergency; in the US, call or text 988. An article — including this one — is information, not assessment, and it is not a plan for your whole life.

## Common questions

### Is catastrophizing the same thing as anxiety?

No. Anxiety is an emotion and, in its disorder forms, a diagnosis. Catastrophizing is a process — a way of processing uncertain situations — that appears inside anxiety, but also inside depression and chronic pain, which is why researchers describe it as a transdiagnostic factor rather than a symptom of any one condition. That distinction is practical, not pedantic: you do not need a diagnosis to work on the process, and having the process does not give you a diagnosis. The chain can be examined link by link by anyone who runs one. When the chain is constant, uncontrollable and shrinking your life, the question changes from process to assessment, and that is the clinician's section above.

### If I stop expecting the worst, won't I be unprepared?

Preparation and rehearsal look similar from inside and are opposites in effect. Preparation ends in a decision or an action: the bag is packed, the appointment is booked, the first step is named. The chain ends in another question. In the Vasey and Borkovec task, the worriers' extra steps did not produce extra information — the content of their chains was much like the nonworriers'; what rose was discomfort and the felt likelihood of the outcomes. Nothing in this guide asks you to drop a real precaution. It asks you to notice the point where the thinking stopped adding preparation and started only adding steps — and to move what remains to the worry period, where the actionable part can be extracted on purpose.

### Why does the worst case feel more likely the longer I think about it?

Because likelihood judgements are not calculations. Butler and Mathews interpreted anxious people's inflated probability ratings through the availability heuristic: an event feels more likely when examples of it come to mind easily. A chain is an availability machine. Each rehearsal makes the scenario easier to picture — more detailed, more fluent, more familiar — and the mind misreads that ease as evidence. Vasey and Borkovec measured the endpoint of that process directly: worriers rated the events in their own catastrophizing sequences as significantly more likely to occur than nonworriers did, on chains whose content was mostly the same. The feeling of likelihood is, in part, a receipt for how long you have been thinking. It is not a reading of the odds.

### What if the bad thing actually could happen?

Then it is a problem to plan for, not a catastrophe to rehearse — and the steps do not change, only their answers do. Some worst cases are real possibilities: results do come back abnormal, jobs do end, people do leave. Decatastrophising never requires pretending the probability is zero. Step 2 asks for the honest probability, the honest cost, and the coping you would actually use; Step 3 asks what information would change your next action, and sends you to get it — including, for anything bodily, a real medical check. What the guide is calibrated against is the inflation: the multiplication that turns a real, copable risk into a certain, total one. If you are in an actual crisis rather than an inflated chain, skip the worksheet logic entirely; the help section is the relevant page.

### How long should I try these steps before judging whether they help?

Judge the pattern across weeks, not the silence of one night. The steps are skills — catching a chain early, separating the judgements, keeping the appointment — and skills start deliberate. The habit research sets the scale: a median of 66 days for a new behaviour to feel automatic, ranging from 18 to 254 days (Lally et al., 2010). You do not need automaticity for the steps to be worth using; a written chain is shorter than an unwritten one the first time you write it. But expect to keep catching yourself mid-chain for a while, and count the honest measures: how many steps the chains run now, how early you catch them, and whether the most-likely sentence is getting easier to reach.

### Can an affirmation app stop catastrophizing?

No — and any app that promises that is overstating what words on a screen can do. An app cannot re-price a probability, resolve an uncertainty, or cope on your behalf. At most, the right words at the right moment can serve the two word-shaped steps: holding the most-likely version where the chain can reach it, and giving a postponed worry somewhere to wait. That is a modest, real function. It is the only one we claim for Anicca, and our measured numbers — printed above, as they are — are the size of the evidence behind the claim so far.
